01.actor: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Akiva and the Elders
01.event: While reclining in the loft of the house of Nit'za in Lod, they are asked whether study or action is greater
01.turn: Rabbi Tarfon says action, Rabbi Akiva says study
01.outcome: All agree study is greater because it leads to action
01.summary: Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders were gathered in an upper room in Lod when a question was put to them: is study or action greater? Tarfon said action, Akiva said study, and all concluded study is greater since it leads to action.
01.missing: Any event beyond the gathering and the exchange of opinions
01.reason: A setting followed by a question and answers is mainly speech; the disagreement and collective resolution give it a little more than ordinary debate, so it sits between borderline and not, and borderline is preferred.

02.event: His relatives, burdened by their stepmother's daily medical costs, come to him for advice
02.turn: He advises them to fix a lump sum with the doctor so the cost comes from her ketuba
02.outcome: He later regrets it, saying he made himself like a legal advisor
02.summary: Rabbi Yohanan's relatives had to pay for their father's widow's daily treatment and came to him. He told them to fix a set fee with the doctor, shifting the cost to her marriage contract. Later he regretted it, saying he had acted like a legal advocate for his own family.
02.reason: An incident, a ruling that changes the outcome, and a subsequent change of heart give more than one event and a change; the Gemara's explanation of his initial and later reasoning is commentary and not part of the story.

03.missing: Any event; only statements by Rav and Rabbi Hiyya about their practice
03.reason: Two sages' statements about why they did not need an eiruv are cited as legal evidence of practice; nothing happens and nothing follows.

04.actor: Ravina and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
04.event: Ravina finds Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door bar, pondering a dilemma
04.summary: Ravina came upon Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak leaning on a door, deep in thought over a legal dilemma about the word 'void'. The question is left unresolved.
04.missing: Any action or change beyond the setting and the question
04.reason: A setting that only frames a legal question is not a story; there is no second event or change.

05.event: Ben Nappaha owned houses in five courtyards in Usha; the case came before the Sages
05.outcome: They ruled that only a place of residence renders carrying prohibited
05.summary: Ben Nappaha had houses in five courtyards in Usha, and the case came before the Sages, who ruled that only his actual residence counts.
05.missing: Any narrated action or change besides bringing the case and the ruling
05.reason: A case brought before rabbis and ruled on, with no other narrated action or change, is not a story under R-C0's limit.

06.actor: Rabbi, Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yohanan, Rav Shemen bar Abba
06.event: Similar cases came before Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael, who ruled differently on sustenance
06.turn: Rabbi Yohanan wonders at one ruling; Rav Shemen reports Shmuel's explanation
06.summary: Two reports (Rav Dimi's and Ravin's) tell of cases before Rabbi and Rabbi Yishmael where sustenance was or was not awarded; Rabbi Yohanan questioned the refusal and Rav Shemen bar Abba cited Shmuel's resolution, to Rabbi Yohanan's astonishment.
06.missing: Narrated incidents beyond 'a case came and he ruled'
06.reason: The incidents are only cases before a rabbi followed by rulings, and the rest is scholarly discussion of those rulings; no other action or change is narrated.

07.actor: A man and his mother; Rabbi
07.event: A man incidentally remarks that he and his mother were captives and he never left her side
07.turn: His unconsidered remark is taken as evidence
07.outcome: Rabbi permits the mother to marry into the priesthood
07.summary: A man, speaking casually, told how he and his mother had been taken captive and that his mind was always on her whether drawing water or gathering wood. On the basis of this remark Rabbi permitted her to marry a priest.
07.missing: The captivity is only reported in his speech; little further action
07.reason: The captivity is a real event and the ruling changes the mother's status, but the passage is essentially a remark followed by a ruling; between borderline and not, borderline is preferred.

08.event: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day after the woman's husband died
08.summary: A man prepared a betrothal feast on the ninetieth day of the widow's waiting period, and Rava made him forfeit it. The Gemara explains it was actually a wedding feast.
08.missing: Detail of the incident; it is only cited as an objection
08.reason: There are two actions and a change (feast prepared, forfeited by Rava), but the incident is only alluded to inside the legal give-and-take, with the Gemara's reinterpretation following.

09.event: A man testifies before Rabbi Ami that someone has presumptive priestly status
09.turn: Rabbi Ami questions the basis; the man notes a Levite read after him
09.outcome: Rabbi Ami elevates the person to priesthood
09.summary: A man came before Rabbi Ami claiming someone was a priest because he read first in the synagogue. Questioned, he explained that a Levite read after him, and Rabbi Ami confirmed the man's priesthood.
09.missing: Any action beyond coming before the rabbi, the questioning and the ruling
09.reason: A case brought to a rabbi, a question and answer, and a ruling: coming before him is the only event, so under R-C0's limit it is not a story.

10.missing: Any event; Rav Yosef's forgetting is only in the translator's gloss
10.reason: Rav Yosef says he never heard the teaching and Abaye reminds him he taught it; this is ordinary scholarly dialogue with no event.

11.missing: Everything after the opening fact: the lost ketuba and what followed are in the context, not the passage
11.reason: The passage states only a family relationship; on its own it narrates nothing.

12.event: Rav Kahana holds an orphan's beer
12.turn: He delays selling it until the Festival despite the risk of souring
12.outcome: He explains it will fetch ready money then
12.summary: Rav Kahana was holding beer belonging to the orphan Rav Mesharshiyya bar Hilkai and held off selling it until the Festival, reasoning that it would bring cash even if it soured a little.
12.missing: Any outcome or change; we are not told what happened to the beer
12.reason: A real action with a stated rationale but no narrated outcome or change; it is close to a bare report of practice, with weak change at most, and borderline is preferred where it sits between.

13.event: He was placed on a seat and his covering tissue was torn open
13.summary: Rabbi Ami cites the tumtum of Biri, who was operated on, torn open, and afterward fathered seven children. Rabbi Yehuda's reply questions whether the children were his.
13.missing: Narrative detail; the incident is cited as an objection in the legal discussion
13.reason: There are real events and a change (operation, then children), but the incident is only alluded to as evidence in the argument rather than narrated.

14.event: Minyamin, a first-generation Egyptian convert, married another first-generation convert
14.outcome: He states he will marry his son to a second-generation convert so his grandson may enter the congregation
14.summary: Rabbi Yehuda reports that his friend Minyamin, an Egyptian convert, said he married a fellow first-generation convert and planned to marry his son to a second-generation convert so that his grandson could join the congregation.
14.missing: Any narrated outcome or change; the future plan is only stated
14.reason: A report of what someone did and planned, cited as halakhic evidence, with nothing following; R-C5 bare report.

15.missing: Any event beyond a question and answer
15.reason: Students ask Rabbi Eliezer a question and he answers; the register settles this very passage (Yevamot 78b:9) as not a story.

16.event: A debtor hid his money by claiming it belonged to a gentile
16.outcome: The Sages acted improperly with him, forcing him to sell his land
16.summary: Asked what actually happened, Rav Hama explains that the debtor had shielded his money by attributing it to a gentile; because he acted improperly, the Sages forced him to sell his land to pay.
16.missing: Narrative detail; the incident is recounted only to explain a ruling
16.reason: There are two actions with causality and a change, but the incident is summarized within a dialogue to clarify a ruling rather than narrated.

17.actor: Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yohanan
17.event: A witness testifies to someone's priesthood before Reish Lakish; Rabbi Elazar challenges Reish Lakish's demand for threshing-floor evidence
17.turn: Later a similar case comes before Rabbi Yohanan, who says the very words Rabbi Elazar said
17.outcome: Reish Lakish looks harshly at Rabbi Elazar and rebukes him for not citing Rabbi Yohanan by name
17.summary: When a man testified before Reish Lakish that someone was a priest, Reish Lakish demanded proof from the threshing floor and Rabbi Elazar objected. Later, sitting before Rabbi Yohanan, the same case arose and Rabbi Yohanan said exactly what Rabbi Elazar had said. Reish Lakish glared at Rabbi Elazar and rebuked him for not quoting the teaching in Rabbi Yohanan's name.
17.reason: Two occasions, a realization and an emotional reaction (the harsh look) with genuine interpersonal conflict give events and change beyond ordinary debate.

18.missing: Any event; only Rav Yosef's statement and Abaye's reminder of a teaching
18.reason: Ordinary scholarly dialogue recalling a halakha; no event or conflict beyond speech.

19.actor: Residents of Sura and Rav Hisda
19.event: Residents placed a rolled mat at the bend of a crooked alleyway as a side post
19.outcome: Rav Hisda declared it ineffective by any opinion
19.summary: In Sura the residents of an L-shaped alley rolled up a mat and set it at the corner as a side post. Rav Hisda ruled that it was valid by neither Rav nor Shmuel, since the wind could blow it over.
19.missing: Any consequence or change after the ruling
19.reason: One action followed by a ruling and legal discussion, with nothing changing afterward; under R-C0 this shape is not a story.

20.event: Rabbi Elazar teaches that the unlearned will not be resurrected; Rabbi Yohanan objects
20.turn: Rabbi Elazar sees that Rabbi Yohanan is grieved
20.outcome: He offers him a remedy from the Torah for the unlearned
20.summary: Rabbi Elazar taught that the unlearned will not rise; Rabbi Yohanan protested that God is not pleased by this. Rabbi Elazar defended it from another verse, but seeing his teacher distressed, he offered a consoling teaching that gives the unlearned a way to merit life.
20.missing: Any event beyond the dialogue and Rabbi Yohanan's distress
20.reason: Mainly speech and exegesis, but there is conflict, an emotional reaction (grief), and a change in Rabbi Elazar's stance in response; borderline under R-C2 and R-C7 shape 1.
